Explain, in one short paragraph, why the sky is blue and why sunsets are red.

The sky appears blue because, as sunlight reaches Earth’s atmosphere, it is scattered in all directions by gas molecules; shorter blue wavelengths scatter more strongly than others, filling the sky with blue light. During a sunset, the sun sits lower on the horizon, forcing its light to travel through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere. This longer path scatters away most of the blue light, leaving only the longer-wavelength reds and oranges to reach your eyes.

The sky appears blue due to Rayleigh scattering, a process where Earth’s atmospheric gases scatter shorter blue wavelengths of sunlight more effectively than other colors. During sunset, the sun is lower on the horizon, forcing its light to travel through a much thicker layer of atmosphere; this causes the blue light to be scattered away entirely before it reaches the observer, leaving only the longer red and orange wavelengths to pass through and color the sky.

Both phenomena are caused by a process called Rayleigh scattering: Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter wavelengths of light (like blue) much more easily than longer wavelengths (like red). During the day, sunlight takes a relatively direct path through the atmosphere, scattering blue light in every direction and making the sky appear blue. At sunset, the sun is low on the horizon, forcing its light to travel through a much thicker layer of atmosphere; this scatters away nearly all the blue light before it can reach your eyes, allowing only the longer, penetrating red and orange wavelengths to pass through.
